teaser: Painted to decorate a guest room. The guest stayed nine weeks and never forgot the walls.

lesson.text: The first person meant to see this picture was another painter. In October 1888 Paul Gauguin stepped off a train in Arles, in the south of France, and was shown to a small bedroom in a yellow house. On the white walls hung sunflowers. His host, Vincent van Gogh, had painted them for him.

Gauguin was hard to impress and stingy with praise. But he told Vincent he liked the sunflowers better than a famous flower piece by Monet. Weeks later, he painted a portrait of his host. He showed him doing one thing: painting sunflowers.

They had been made in a rush two months earlier. Cut sunflowers droop within hours, so Vincent started at sunrise and worked without stopping, finishing four canvases in about a week. This one, the largest bunch, holds fifteen blooms. They are not all the same age.

lesson.title: Three ages of a flower
lesson.text: One vase, several moments of a life.

spots.title: In bloom
spots.text: This one faces you with a full collar of petals, each a single curved stroke of yellow. The dark eye at its center is only a few dabs of brown and blue.

spots.title: Gone to seed
spots.text: The petals have dropped. What remains is the heavy seed head, a rough ball of ochre with a green heart. Most of the flowers in the vase are at this stage.

spots.title: Collapsing
spots.text: Here the head hangs sideways on a bent stalk and the petals have shriveled into twisting strands. This flower is nearly finished.

lesson.text: So the bouquet is less a still life than a clock. Bud, bloom, seed, wilt: a whole summer, pressed into one jug. Dutch painters of earlier centuries used flowers to hint that life is short. Vincent, who was Dutch, keeps that old idea and sets it on fire with color.
He wrote to his brother Theo that he was painting them “with the gusto of a Marseillais eating bouillabaisse”, the garlicky fish stew of the nearby port of Marseille.

The color was the real experiment. Yellow flowers in a yellow pot on a yellow table against a yellow wall. Any art teacher would have told him to add a dark background so the blooms stand out. He wanted to prove a picture could be built from one color in many voices, from pale lemon to burnt orange.
With so little contrast of color, something else has to separate petal from wall and pot from table. He uses the paint itself, and one unexpected line.

lesson.title: How it holds together
lesson.text: Where yellow meets yellow, look at the surface.

spots.title: Paint like clay
spots.text: The seed heads are built from thick blobs pushed on with a loaded brush, so they stand up from the canvas. Real light catches them and casts tiny real shadows.

spots.title: A woven wall
spots.text: The background is not flat. Short strokes cross each other like basketwork, in a paler, cooler yellow that sits back behind the flowers.

spots.title: The blue line
spots.text: A single wobbly stroke of blue marks where table ends and wall begins. Blue is yellow's opposite, so this thin line makes both yellows glow.

lesson.text: That thick, raised paint has a name: impasto. Most painters before him smoothed their brushwork away. Vincent leaves every stroke showing, so you can follow the speed and direction of his hand, as if the picture were still being made.

The yellows have changed. He relied on a new factory-made pigment called chrome yellow, and scientists have found that some of it slowly darkens toward brown in light. The painting Gauguin saw was probably brighter than the one we have.
He was proud enough of this canvas to sign it, which he did for only a minority of his pictures. But he did not put his name in a corner. He hid it inside the scene, as part of an object.

spots.title: Vincent
spots.text: On the jug, in blue, like a potter's mark: just “Vincent”. He dropped his surname because, he said, people in France could not pronounce Van Gogh.

lesson.text: The shared house lasted nine weeks. The two men argued about everything, and just before Christmas, after a violent quarrel, Vincent cut off part of his own ear and Gauguin left for Paris. From there Gauguin wrote to ask if he could have one of the sunflower paintings. Vincent painted copies instead.

Not everyone was charmed. At an exhibition in Brussels in 1890, a Belgian painter refused to hang his work in the same room as the sunflowers and insulted them at dinner. Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec, who was there, challenged him to a duel. It was called off.

Vincent died that same year, having sold almost nothing. His sister-in-law Jo kept the pictures and spent decades making him known. In 1924 she agreed, reluctantly, to sell this canvas to the National Gallery in London. She wrote that it was a sacrifice made for the sake of his glory.
Sunflowers shows that a painting can run on a single color. Variety comes from tone, from texture, and from one well-placed line of the opposite hue.

spots.title: The wild one
spots.text: Petals fly off in every direction and green leaves spike out behind them. Its dark center is dotted with thick specks of seeds.

spots.title: The red eye
spots.text: The flower at the heart of the bunch has an orange-red center ringed in dark line, like a target. It is the warmest spot on the canvas.

spots.title: At the edge
spots.text: This seed head pushes right up against the frame, with a pale green bud dangling below it. The bouquet is almost too big for the canvas.

spots.title: Almost over
spots.text: The lowest flower on the left has turned pale green and droops below the level of the vase's rim. Thin, wiry strokes are all that is left of its petals.

spots.title: Green against orange
spots.text: Dark green leaves cut across this hanging bloom, outlined in blue. It is the strongest contrast in the lower half of the picture.

spots.title: The glint
spots.text: A few touches of white on the jug's shoulder are enough to make the glazed pottery shine.

lesson.text: In October 2022 two climate protesters threw a can of tomato soup over the painting in London. It hangs behind glass and was unharmed, apart from light damage to the frame, and was back on the wall the same day.

quiz.question: For whom did Van Gogh paint the sunflowers?
quiz.explanation: They were made to decorate the room of his guest, Gauguin.

quiz.question: Why did he have to paint so fast?
options: He was about to leave Arles
He had run out of money for canvas
quiz.explanation: The flowers drooped quickly, so he started at sunrise and worked without stopping.

quiz.question: What is impasto?
options: Paint applied so thickly it stands up from the canvas
quiz.explanation: The seed heads are built from thick, raised paint.

quiz.question: What separates the table from the wall?
options: A change from yellow to green
quiz.explanation: One wobbly blue stroke marks the edge and makes the yellows glow.

quiz.question: How did he sign the painting?
options: “V. van Gogh” in the bottom corner
quiz.explanation: The first name alone sits on the vase like a potter's mark.

quiz.question: What has happened to some of the yellow paint over time?
quiz.explanation: Some chrome yellow slowly darkens in light.

facts.text: All the sunflowers in the vase are shown at the same stage of bloom.
facts.explanation: The bunch mixes fresh blooms, seed heads and wilting flowers.

facts.text: Toulouse-Lautrec once challenged a painter to a duel for insulting the sunflowers.
facts.explanation: It happened at an exhibition dinner in Brussels in 1890, and was called off.

facts.text: Van Gogh sold this canvas himself to the National Gallery.
facts.explanation: His sister-in-law Jo sold it to the gallery in 1924, long after his death.
